title: Appendix C: Security, Privacy, and Cost Review

sections.title: Privacy and the Life of Personal Data

html:
Appendix C: Security, Privacy, and Cost Review

The main chapters go deep on capacity, state, and recovery, and they leave three other constraints at the edge of the page. Security, privacy, and cost can each stop a design that works from shipping, and each yields to the same discipline the rest of the book uses: state the assumption, name the evidence, say who owns it, and record what happens if it is wrong.

Use this appendix to identify security, privacy, and cost questions during a design review. Record unresolved questions and assign them to the relevant security, legal, or finance specialist.

Security

We start with authorization, asking where it is actually checked. A check at the edge is not enough. The resource itself should verify that the authenticated actor, taken from trusted request context, may touch that particular record, because a well-formed identifier can belong to another customer (Chapters 3 and 13). Calls between services deserve the same care: they should authenticate a service identity, and a network address is not one.

Next, examine what happens when an authorization, rate-limit, or feature-flag lookup fails. If the authorization service is slow, does the caller allow the request or deny it? Either answer can be right, depending on what the request does. The defect is choosing without noticing that a choice was made.

Then look at credentials. List the ones each service holds and what each would allow an attacker to do if it leaked. Scope them to the smallest set of resources that works, and rehearse rotation before you need it (Chapter 6). The same thinking applies to everything a service accepts without validation: queue messages, events, webhooks, model output, and retrieved documents are all inputs, and each needs validation of structure and authority, as Chapter 13 described for tool calls.

Two more places repay a look. The build artifact should pin its base images and dependencies by digest or version, and someone should know who can publish to the registry (Chapter 6). Recovery tooling needs care too, because replay tools, manual status overrides, and emergency allocations are privileged operations, and they should leave audit records naming the actor and the operation (Appendix A).

Privacy and the Life of Personal Data

The most useful privacy exercise is to follow one piece of personal data from the moment it enters the system to every place a copy ends up. The primary database is only the beginning. Copies appear in caches, search indexes, event logs, analytics stores, feature stores, training sets, backups, and logs, and most privacy defects live in the copies that never reached the diagram.

Logs and traces deserve particular suspicion, because request bodies, tokens, and identifiers end up in them easily and they have their own retention. Customer identifiers belong in access-controlled records, not in metric labels (Chapter 8). For every store, write down how long data stays. Then check that the longest-lived copy, often a backup or an event log, fits the promise made to customers.

Deletion is the hardest part, because a request to delete has to reach every derived copy. Chapters 11, 12, and 13 each created one: a projection, an event log, a feature store, a training set. For each one, define how a deletion reaches it and which record shows that the deletion was applied. The same goes for location. Regional rules and contracts limit where data may be processed (Chapter 14), and the limit includes third-party processors and inference providers, which receive whatever the prompt contains.

Cost

Cost is a design constraint in the same sense that latency is. A design that meets every objective at ten times the affordable price has failed, and the financial effect may not appear until a later reporting period.

The useful unit is the cost of one completed customer outcome. Cost per call understates it, because outcomes often need several calls. The multipliers to look for are the ones this book has already named: retries, fan-out, cache misses, repeated tool calls, recovery reserves, and telemetry volume.

Here is the arithmetic for an assistant that handles 10 million requests a day and averages 1.4 model calls per request, as in the repeated-search example of Chapter 13. Each call has a 1,200-token prompt and a 300-token response. Take hypothetical prices of $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, which are not any provider’s prices but are chosen to make the arithmetic easy to follow.

\[\begin{aligned} \text{input, per call} &= 1{,}200 \times \frac{\$3}{10^{6}} = \$0.0036,\\ \text{output, per call} &= 300 \times \frac{\$15}{10^{6}} = \$0.0045,\\ \text{per call} &= \$0.0081,\\ \text{per day} &= 10^{7}\times 1.4 \times \$0.0081 = \$113{,}400. \end{aligned}\]

Now every design decision has a price. Trimming the prompt by a quarter changes the input term. A retry policy that adds ten percent more calls adds more than $11,000 a day. A cache in front of the model changes the call count; none of these shows up on a latency dashboard.

Telemetry has a price as well. The number of time series a metric produces is the product of its label values. A request counter labeled by 12 endpoints, 5 status classes, and 200 instances produces 12,000 series. Add a customer identifier with two million values and the potential count rises to \(2.4\times10^{10}\). The bill arrives long before the dashboard loads.

Insurance is a cost too. The payment design in Chapter 14 reserves 45 of its 200 provider calls, or 22.5 percent, for captures, reconciliation, and emergencies. That capacity sits idle in normal operation. It is the price of being able to recover, and it should appear in the review as a cost accepted on purpose.
